title: The intermediate scattering function of an interacting adlayer as a characteristic function: a closed-form theory of Ising lattice-gas surface diffusion
abstract: The intermediate scattering function (ISF) measured by helium spin-echo is a characteristic function (CF): the Fourier transform of the distribution of adsorbate displacements, whose value at zero time is the static structure factor. We use this double role to bring lateral interactions of Ising lattice-gas type into surface diffusion. The ISF then follows in closed form in momentum transfer, time, coverage and temperature, and with it the whole linear-response hierarchy. A single correlation parameter fixes both the equilibrium structure and the interaction-renormalized hop rate; it is exact along a one-dimensional channel, and is carried onto the surface as the nearest-neighbour correlation of a pair approximation, the momentum dependence of the structure factor then coming from a collective (random-phase) treatment. The closed form is not postulated. Projecting the master equation onto the density gives an exact equation of motion whose amplitude is an identity and whose initial rate obeys a sum rule, so that the quasi-elastic weight is the layer's own structure factor and de Gennes narrowing becomes a theorem rather than an analogy; the closed form is what remains when the memory kernel of that equation is dropped. Kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) on the same Hamiltonian reproduces the dressed hop rate to better than about one per cent and the initial collective rate to $1$--$2\%$. Four correlated, non-critical fingerprints of the interaction follow --- in the quasi-elastic amplitude, its linewidth, the Arrhenius slope, and the dependence of the fitted linewidth on the range of times over which the decay is fitted. They invert in closed form for the attempt frequency, the static barrier and the interaction. Applications to Na/Cu(111) and H/Pt(111) are analysed and discussed.
summary: This paper presents a closed-form theory for the intermediate scattering function of an interacting adlayer, treating it as an Ising lattice-gas system. By leveraging the ISF's role as a characteristic function, the authors successfully incorporate lateral interactions into surface diffusion dynamics. The resulting theory provides testable predictions that are validated against Kinetic Monte Carlo simulations.
main_problem: To develop a closed-form theoretical description for the intermediate scattering function (ISF) of an interacting adlayer undergoing surface diffusion.
main_result: The authors derived a closed-form expression for the ISF that rigorously incorporates lateral interactions, predicting four correlated fingerprints observable in experimental measurements.
method: The theory utilizes the characteristic function framework, projecting the master equation onto the density and employing techniques like Random-Phase Approximation (RPA) and Transfer Matrix methods to derive exact or controlled approximations.
model_or_system: The system is an interacting adlayer modeled as an Ising lattice-gas on a substrate. Dynamics are governed by surface diffusion processes, analyzed via measurements like helium spin-echo yielding the ISF.
key_observables: Intermediate Scattering Function (ISF), $I(K, t)$; Static Structure Factor, $F(K)$; Quasi-elastic line shape; Linewidth and Arrhenius slope dependence on coverage.
important_parameters: Interaction strength ($\varepsilon$), temperature ($T$), adsorbate coverage ($	heta$), momentum transfer ($K$).
main_assumptions: The closed form is obtained by dropping the memory kernel of the equation of motion, which provides a controlled approximation; the RPA is used for 2D treatment.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the deviation parameter $\Delta(K)$ across the zone for different interaction regimes and test theoretical bounds against KMC data to validate the closed-form applicability.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the ISF as a characteristic function, develops the theory using lattice gas models (1D via Transfer Matrix, 2D via RPA), derives the closed form by controlling approximations, and validates these results through comparison with KMC simulations and specific physical applications (Na/Cu(111)).
why_interesting: The rigorous derivation of dynamics from static structure factors using a characteristic function approach is highly relevant for understanding non-equilibrium many-body systems where memory effects are crucial.

Here the transfer-matrix statics and Γeff are exact, so the test isolates the Markovian truncation. (a) Statics: F(K) = I(K, 0) from simulation (points) against the exact Lorentzian (20) (line). Figure 4: The same benchmark on a square lattice (z = 4, θ = 0.5, βε = −0.8, along Γ→M), testing what the channel cannot: here neither the statics nor Γeff is exact. (a) Statics: the measured F (points) lies between the random-phase form (32) (solid), which overestimates the correlation peak, and the pair-approximation Lorentzian (20) (dashed). (b) Dynamics: the collective rate built from the measured F (points) follows the closed form (solid) to 10–15%, while the tagged-particle rate (open squares) falls below the mean-rate form (dashed) by the tracer correlation factor fc ≈0.7–0.9 that the theory omits.
